newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sees Clinton visit as sign to NATO sceptics.
newsitem.headline: Poland sees Clinton visit as sign to NATO sceptics.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's visit to Poland after the Madrid summit next month will be an important signal to those in the United States who are undecided about or opposed to the expansion of NATO, the Polish president said on Friday.

White House officials earlier said Clinton had decided to visit Poland, one of the three countries that the United States has backed for an invitation to start NATO entry talks at the July 8-9 alliance summit.

"This will be important both for Poland and for the United States and for those who in America are still not decided," President Aleksander Kwasniewski told public radio in an interview, adding that Clinton would probably be in Warsaw on July 10.
Kwasniewski said Clinton wanted to show commitment to ending divisions in Europe dating from the Yalta and Potsdam meetings between Western and Soviet World War Two leaders.

"This will show American opinion instantly that something important and historic has happened and must be carried through, because in the United States there are sceptics and even opponents of enlarging NATO," Kwasniewski said.
He said the sight and words of their president in Warsaw, rebuilt from its wartime ruins and now at last able to enjoy security with democracy, would sway U.S. public opinion.
"Americans often understand more through symbols than through long lectures," Kwasniewski said.

He said Poland not only had to improve its army and maintain political stability and economic development to ensure its place in NATO, it also had to persuade two thirds of U.S. senators to ratify its admission, which is expected in 1999.
"This battle has not ended, it still awaits us," he said. @

The Polish leader rejected arguments in Thursday's open letter to Clinton from about 50 ex-senators and other pillars of the U.S. foreign policy establishment. The letter called for NATO enlargement to be postponed to explore other options.
It argued that expanding NATO now would play into the hands of the non-democratic opposition in Russia and undermine proponents there of reform and cooperation with the West.

Kwasniewski branded the argument illogical, saying it would leave Poland and central Europe in a grey zone of European security if imperial tendencies revived in Russia, dominant state in the former Soviet Union whose Warsaw Pact alliance enclosed much of central and eastern Europe including Poland.

"If in Russia at some moment those non-democratic forces win and take power and an attempt begins to build an imperial policy, will Poland then be taken into NATO in 24 hours? Or not at all?" Kwasniewski said.
Clinton has said he favours admitting Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic into the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in what he hopes will be the first of a series of enlargements.
He is also due to visit Romania next month to reassure its people that their country is an excellent candidate for the next round of NATO expansion.
